goal.heading: 1. What Is the Goal of This Toolkit?
paragraphs: The goal of this toolkit is to reduce suicidal ideation among youth served through the Rise short-term treatment model. It does this by supporting the therapists who work with them: consolidating practical, evidence-informed tools in one place and by providing resources, tips and strategies to make your day-to-day practice easier, more efficient, and more connected.

Rather than replacing clinical judgment or training, it's meant to give therapists a clear roadmap, vetted resources, guidance for working with schools, and support for their own sustainability in this rewarding, yet challenging, work.

how.heading: 3. How Was This Toolkit Developed?
how.intro: We listened to your experiences and collaboratively designed solutions to address your needs. We used a framework called the Discover, Design, Build, Test model.

pairs.solution: We know 12 sessions is short. That's why we built this toolkit. Developed with therapists, clinical and research experts in youth suicide prevention, the Treatment Roadmap structures our brief model around what matters most in a short window: reducing risk and stabilizing crisis, building emotion regulation, problem-solving and support seeking skills, and building a life worth living, all in service of reducing suicidal ideation.

pairs.concern: We spend too much time looking for resources.
pairs.solution: We have created a vetted Treatment Library for you to pull from. Search for exactly what you need to help clients link to resources in the community, referrals for therapy after your treatment wraps, and access a library of evidence-based worksheets and tools to use in therapy with youth, families and schools.

pairs.concern: Working in the schools is complicated.
pairs.solution: We have built a school navigation page filled with resources to support your work in schools. We have a list of questions for you to ask schools to get to know the lay of the land, we have tips for navigating tricky interactions, and suggestions for collaborating with schools to best support youth and families.

pairs.concern: This work takes a personal toll.
pairs.solution: Working with youth at risk for suicide is some of the hardest clinical work there is. These tools help you spot burnout early, build resilience into your practice, provide you with tips and tricks for your peers, and allow you to schedule a consultation call with our licensed clinical psychologist.

useIt.heading: 5. How Do I Use This Toolkit?
useIt.intro: This toolkit is designed to be flexible: use what works for you, your clients and your workflow. Here are some suggestions:

guidance.title: Start with the Treatment Roadmap.
guidance.body: Use it to help you plan and deliver your therapy. Revisit session by session to see where you are and what comes next.

guidance.title: Dip into the Treatment Library when you need something specific.
guidance.body: Align it with the Roadmap, and treat it like a search tool: pull a handout for a family session, grab an assessment before intake, or find a referral when treatment is wrapping up.

guidance.title: Turn to Navigating Schools before or during any school-facing work.
guidance.body: Review the sample questions ahead of a school meeting, or reference the role-clarification tips when a case starts to feel tangled between systems.

guidance.title: Revisit Therapist Self-Care regularly, not just when things feel hard.
guidance.body: Build a check-in by integrating these tools into your own routine - weekly, monthly, whatever's sustainable - so you catch signs of strain early rather than after burnout sets in.

tips: You don't need to use every tool with every client. Pick what's relevant to the case in front of you.
Tools can be adapted. Use your clinical judgment to fit language, pacing, and content to each youth and family.
Come back often. This is meant to be a living resource you return to throughout a case, not a one-time read!
If you want support, or to talk through a case, remember you can also schedule a consultation call with our licensed clinical psychologist.

closing.pre: If you have suggestions to improve our toolkit, please let us know!
closing.post: The goal is to support you best – we need your help knowing how to do this!

schoolsPage.heading: Navigating Schools
schoolsPage.intro: We've heard from therapists that navigating schools is one of the most complex and challenging parts of this job. Based on therapist input, we've put together tips for working with schools, plus practical tools to keep key school information handy over the course of treatment.

quote.text: We're definitely navigating 50 systems every time we walk into a school.

tips.title: Find and connect with a school partner
tips.body: When a youth requests for sessions to occur in the school through Rise, the Rise therapist reaches out to the QRS (qualified referral source): the person who entered the referral. This is often the Mental Health Advocate, School Counselor, Interventionist, or School Social Worker. This person can help determine the best time to meet with the youth based on their school schedule, and where sessions can be held. The Rise therapist is expected to communicate with the QRS at least 24 hours before coming to the school to meet with the youth.

tips.title: Connect with your school partner and answer key questions
tips.body: Use the interview guide below to get your important questions about working in the school answered. The goal is to equip you with what you need to understand the specific school context and work effectively there. Each time you start working in a new school, find a school contact for a brief meeting or phone call to go through these questions. Your answers save in this browser and carry over to Your Client's School Card.

tips.title: Clarify the roles of school personnel, the Rise therapist, and Rise admin
tips.body: Youth and families may be confused about the roles of the school and their therapist, and may or may not know about the role of Rise admin. Give young people clear information about roles and confidentiality. You can open the discussion by asking whether they've heard of confidentiality before and exploring what they think it means. Validate that it can be hard to keep track of all the adults involved in their care, and provide psychoeducation about each role.

tips.title: Get a Release of Information to communicate with the youth's school
tips.body: We strongly suggest getting a signed release of information (ROI) form from the youth and family so you can exchange information with the client's school.

tips.title: Learn the school's policies and practices
tips.body: We are developing a set of policies, practices, and insider tips for working in the schools we serve. More soon!

tips.title: Be prepared to support youth through school re-entry after a crisis
tips.body: Youth with suicidal thoughts and behaviors often move in and out of schools and other systems of care. A supported return to school helps protect the progress made in reducing suicidal ideation, so be prepared to support youth through these transitions.

guidelines.heading: Rise School Guidelines
guidelines.intro: When seeing Rise clients in the school setting, the Rise provider is a representative of Rise Against Suicide. Follow the school's policies and procedures, as well as the Rise protocol below.
items: The QRS is the only school staff member the Rise provider communicates with at the school. Never reach out to the principal or a school administrator unless directed to by the QRS.
Rise providers do not speak on behalf of Rise in the school setting unless Rise staff are present or have arranged it.
Regular communication between the Rise provider and the QRS is encouraged while the client is progressing through sessions.
For a Rise provider to see a youth, the Rise referral process must be completed in the Rise RMS or through a Rise staff member.
If the client has a social service need, the school counselor or appropriate school staff may be notified to help the student.
Give the QRS at least 24 hours' notice before arriving to see a client at the school, including arranging a place to meet the student.
Sign in at the front desk and ask for the QRS who contacted you.
Immediately report any concerns about the young person to the QRS, and collaborate on school policies and procedures.
Respond within 24 hours on business days to QRS outreach about availability and fit.
Rise providers are not available to school staff for consultation services as part of the Rise program.

options.hint: The original arrangement and flat lines, but factors in the same ring share one pill, so there are never more than 5 pills per side.

options.hint: One pill per factor, ordered from the outer ring (Community) at the top to the inner ring (Client) at the bottom.

steps.ring: As you map this level, ask: what here raises or lowers the client's suicidal ideation?
steps.topFactors: Choose the factors most closely tied to the client's suicidal ideation. These become the focus of treatment.
steps.resourcePlan: Pick interventions that directly target what drives the client's suicidal ideation, or strengthen what protects against it.
steps.review: Every phase of this plan works toward one outcome: reducing the client's suicidal ideation.

phases.focus: Understand what is driving the client's suicidal ideation, and keep them safe while you work on it. Assess current risk, build a safety plan together, and map the factors that raise and lower it.
phases.check: Do I know what is driving this client's suicidal ideation, and is a safety plan in place?

phases.focus: Give the client skills to manage suicidal thoughts when they show up and lower them over time. Teach and practice emotion regulation, problem-solving, and support-seeking, aimed at the top factors you identified.
phases.check: Is the client using these skills when suicidal thoughts or urges come up?

phases.focus: Make the reduction in suicidal ideation last after Rise ends. Consolidate skills, re-screen to measure change since intake, update the safety plan, and link the client to their next step in care.
phases.check: Has the client's suicidal ideation decreased since intake, and is care in place to keep it that way?

safetyPlanPage.heading: Make A Safety Plan
safetyPlanPage.intro: Build a personalized safety plan step by step, together with the client, to help them stay safe through moments of suicidal ideation. Each step focuses on one part of the plan — add as many items as apply, then review the whole plan before printing a copy for the client to keep.
safetyPlanPage.crisisBanner: If you or someone you know is in immediate danger, call 911. You can also call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, available 24/7.
safetyPlanPage.disclaimer: This tool is a starting point for completing the Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention together with a client. It saves only in this browser — nothing is sent anywhere.

steps.heading: My Warning Signs
steps.intro: A warning sign is something the client thinks, feels, or does as suicidal thoughts are starting to develop.
steps.placeholder: e.g. trouble sleeping, pulling away from friends

steps.heading: My Coping Strategies
steps.intro: Coping strategies are things the client can do on their own to feel a little better in the moment, without needing to contact anyone else.
steps.placeholder: e.g. listen to music, go for a walk, draw

steps.heading: My Distractions
steps.intro: Distractions are people or places that may offer comfort or help the client take a break from the situation, so they can start feeling or thinking differently.
steps.placeholder: e.g. a friend's house, the school gym

steps.heading: My Supports
steps.intro: Supports are people the client feels comfortable talking to about what they're going through, and who can help. When possible, it helps to talk with them about being a support before a crisis happens.
steps.placeholder: e.g. a parent, sibling, coach, or friend

steps.heading: My Professional Supports
steps.intro: Professional contacts are people who can provide professional care and support, including therapists, doctors, and crisis lines.
steps.placeholder: e.g. therapist name and phone number

steps.heading: My Safer Environment
steps.intro: Having items nearby that could be used for self-harm can be dangerous during a crisis. What items might need to be stored safely, given to someone else, or removed — and how?
steps.placeholder: e.g. ask a parent to store medications

research.heading: Discover. Design. Test.
research.intro: This toolkit is being co-designed through a rigorous, community-engaged research process with Rise therapists — not built for them, but with them.

aims.title: Discover
aims.body: Focus groups and interviews with 10 Rise therapists, analyzed across 9 domains covering strengths, challenges, interventions, and toolkit vision.

aims.title: Design & Build
aims.body: Two two-session co-design workshop sequences with Rise therapists, creating and refining toolkit prototypes based on real needs.

aims.title: Test
aims.body: Mixed-method pilot testing through interviews and surveys with community therapists to assess feasibility and acceptability.

quotes.text: We go to them. They choose us, we work for them.
I feel like it's almost impossible to work with kids and not also work with their parents.
I literally bring in several handouts from DBT, CBT, because I don't know how much time I'm going to have with that person.
Be another trusted adult that's not their parents, that's not gonna judge them — really just give space to listen.
A community, like, maybe a therapist forum or something.
Having some sort of list or… if there was a provider database… and it's all in one.

team.heading: Community-Engaged Research
team.intro: This project is a collaboration between the University of Colorado Boulder and Rise Against Suicide, funded through community-engaged scholarship.

members.title: University of Colorado Boulder
members.body: Led by Dr. Tamar, Assistant Professor in Psychology and Neuroscience. Research-driven co-design, qualitative analysis, and evidence-based resource development.
